subject: chemistry
title: Equilibrium Adventure 3: Kc, Kp and ΔG at equilibrium
welcome_lead: Today you'll connect Kc to ΔG via the Gibbs equation.
meta_desc: Chemistry HL — relationship Kc ↔ Kp, ΔG = -RT ln K, feasibility.
final_note: You learned ΔG = -RT ln K; spontaneous when K > 1 (negative ΔG); Kp from partial pressures, Kc from concentrations.

concepts.def: Q < K → forward; Q > K → reverse

walkthroughs.body_html:
For gases, Kp uses partial pressures instead of concentrations.

p(A) × V = n(A)RT, so [A] = p(A)/RT.

Kp = Kc · (RT)^Δn where Δn = (moles gas product) - (moles gas reactant).

ΔG° = -RT ln K

- K = 1 → ΔG° = 0 (equilibrium 50:50).
- K > 1 → ΔG° < 0 → spontaneous as written.
- K < 1 → ΔG° > 0 → non-spontaneous (reverse spontaneous).

At any moment, Q has the same form as K but with current concentrations.

- Q < K → reaction goes forward.
- Q > K → reaction goes reverse.
- Q = K → no net change (at equilibrium).

ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q. At Q = K, ΔG = 0.

mcqs.q: Kp and Kc are related by Kp = Kc × (RT)^Δn where Δn refers to:
What are the units of Kc for a reaction?
options: A catalyst decreases Kc by stabilising the reactants.
They depend on Δn (the difference between moles of gaseous/aqueous products and reactants) — Kc can be dimensionless or have units like mol dm^-3.
Kc always has units of mol dm^-3.

mcqs.q: Does adding a catalyst change the value of Kc?
options: A catalyst increases Kc by favouring product formation.
No — a catalyst speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so Kc is unchanged.
A catalyst decreases Kc by stabilising the reactants.

mcqs.q: What does Kp use instead of concentrations?
options: Partial pressures of each gaseous component at equilibrium.
Kp uses the total pressure of the system raised to the stoichiometric coefficients.
Kp uses the volumes of each gas in the mixture.
